verification.reason: holds() at parity.ts:465 compares the whole claim string, `${pid} ${uuid}\n`. The UUID is the only part that tells two runs with the same pid apart. The two tests that reach this check don't exercise that. One replaces the lock with "999 other\n" (test line 1019). The other deletes the lock (line 1038). "999" differs from process.pid, so a pid-only comparison (the mutation described) would still reject both. The test at line 1567 only matches the lock's format. I found no test that writes a lock with the same pid and a different UUID. A mutant that dropped the UUID from the comparison would pass the whole suite, and the pid-reuse case it guards against would go unchecked.

verification.correction: Validate the lock before echoing it. For example, lstat it and require a regular file, or print the content only if it matches /^\d+$/. Otherwise omit it from the message.

lowered.reason: Exploitation needs local write access to the results directory, or control of the output setting, to plant the symlink. The disclosed text is printed only to the running operator's own stderr, not returned to the attacker, so it matters only where the logs are shared, such as CI. The code also prints only the part of the target before the first space, and the target must be readable by the process (parity.ts:453-456, 425-427).

verification.reason: The probe failed again and exercises the real path: measureParity, then ResultsLock.take. When writeFileSync with the wx flag hits EEXIST, including on a planted symlink, the handler calls readFileSync(path) and puts the first space-delimited field of the target into the error message. measureHeld prints that message through printError. Nothing checks that the lock is a regular file, that its content is a PID, or that the target is not a symlink. Base had no ResultsLock, so the head introduced this read. The leak is real, but the attacker has to plant a symlink next to the results path, and the output goes only to the operator's own console or logs.
